title: The Case of the Missing Light
markdown:
The clubhouse at the edge of Whispering Woods had always been a little proud of its lantern. It hung from a beam above the story-cushion, and on good evenings it made the knot-holes look like friendly eyes. On a blustery autumn afternoon the lantern decided it had had enough of being proud. Wind worried the shutters. Inside, the cheerful beacon dwindled to a weak flickering ember, sulked, and left Owen the gardener squinting at a drawing of the giant oak that might as well have been a rumour.

Owen’s curiosity usually bloomed brighter than any sunflower. Today it furrowed, like a field that had been ploughed in the wrong direction. He pushed his spectacles up his nose and gave the lantern a tap that was more hope than engineering.

“Fiddlesticks. It’s barely enough light to see the whiskers on your face. We can’t even see our best drawing of the giant oak, and tomorrow is the big storytelling night.”

Lyra the moth shimmered on his sleeve, wings like dusted velvet. Her own small glow dimmed in sympathy. She nudged his hand with an antenna: well?

He lifted the lantern. It gave a last pathetic sputter, a puff of grey, and went out. The wooden walls, which liked chatter, went thick and quiet. Lyra shivered, not from cold.

A whistle arrived from the path, bright as a robin. Engineer Saira’s toolbelt jingled. She took in Owen’s slump and Lyra’s droop.

“Clubhouse blues? Has your grand lantern packed its light for the season?”

Owen explained the dimming, the sputter, the way the oak drawing had vanished into evening. Saira nodded, thought in her brow, play in her eye. She knelt so the lantern was a puzzle on the floor between them, not a disappointment hanging out of reach.

“A lack of illumination. Don’t fret, my little adventurers. Every dimming light has a spark hiding in it.”

While she turned the lantern in her hands, Owen’s gaze drifted to a fallen branch by the door. A jewel-beetle blinked there. Oddly, the blink sharpened when the beetle walked a patch of moss stitched with almost invisible silver threads, like miniature cobwebs.

“Lyra — look. Its light gets stronger on that mossy bit. As if the moss gives it extra oomph.”

Saira’s face lit, which was useful in a dark clubhouse. “You’ve spotted a path, Owen. That beetle has found a way for its spark to travel. Our lantern needs a proper path for its energy too. Battery. Switch. Bulb. Roads in between.”

From the belt: a small smooth object, faintly warm. “Battery. Tiny energy, tucked away. These—” two twisty strands “—are wires. Roads. This clicky thing is a switch. A gatekeeper. It decides when the energy may go for a walk.”

She held a glass bulb. One wire from battery to bulb. Nothing. The glass stayed sulky.

Owen glanced at the beetle. “But the moss—”

“A complete path,” Saira said. “Watch.”

A second wire, bulb back to battery, a loop. The energy ran out, through, back. The bulb woke. “A circuit,” she named it, because a loop that works deserves a short name.

Owen’s spectacles caught the new gold. Lyra buzzed a circle and threw tiny rainbows on the walls.

“A complete path,” Owen said, standing straighter, as if he had grown an inch of wire himself.

“Now you two. Snug connections. No floppy roads.”

Owen’s fingers, gardener-steady, found the battery. Lyra’s antennae guided a wire to the bulb with moth precision. Saira showed the switch as a gate. Owen breathed. Click.

Warmth poured into the clubhouse, brighter than memory, brighter even than the lantern in its boastful days. The oak drawing came back leaf by leaf, branch by branch. They could see the little owl Owen had hidden in the foliage, and Lyra’s favourite smudge of moon. Treasures along the shelf remembered they had edges. Lyra looped the air, a tiny aerial ballet. Owen clapped once, then again, because once was not enough for a room that had been mist.

“Hooray,” he said, because some words are circuits too: they only work if you complete them out loud.

Saira’s belt settled. “Electricity likes a circle. Gate open: it flows, the light works. Gate shut: it waits. That is how we use batteries and wires and switches without drama. Complete path. Never touch bare wires while the battery is connected. Energy should know where to go, and where to come home.”

Owen looked at the lantern, then at Lyra, then at the moss outside, where the beetle had taken its spark elsewhere. He did not need a speech about secrets in plain sight. He had a drawing he could see, a switch he could click, and a moth who insisted on inspecting the bulb from every angle, as if light might need a second opinion.

Storytelling night would have a lantern that stayed. Owen coiled the spare wire the way he coiled garden twine, neat enough for tomorrow’s hands. Lyra settled on the warm hood of the lantern and dimmed her own glow, which is moth for job done. In the woods the wind kept blustering. Inside, the circuit held its round, small and complete, and the giant oak on the wall looked, at last, like a tree.
